utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before the witness will be brought into the courtroom, I'd like to say that yesterday, when I rendered the Chamber's decision on the exhibits tendered through the witness after Avramovic, I mistakenly referred to annexes 7 through 11 to Mr. Afterramvic Rule 92 ter statement as being exhibits P130 through P134. This, you'll find, on page 7447. The correct exhibit numbers for these annexes are P390 through 394. And they should be admitted under those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fazliu. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. I take it that that's clear to you. Today you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence of the accused, that is, counsel for Mr. Haradinaj, counsel for Mr. Balaj, and counsel for Mr. Brahimaj. Mr. Emmerson, as far as policy for private session is concerned, the same applies as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Given the approach that has been taken thus far, I think it might be wise if we begin in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I'm going to show you some documents in this file and then ask you some questions about them. But first of all, just so you that you understand what is in the file, behind tab 1 is the Albanian original, then an English translation of a newspaper article published in Bota Sot newspaper on the 15th of March 2005, very shortly after the indictment in this case was made public and, of course, mentioned your name. Behind tab 2, you have first an Albanian and then an English translation of a witness statement made and signed by yourself when interviewed by investigators for the Defence on the 15th of June. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, when you were interviewed by the Defence investigators, you were given your statement in the Albanian original so that you could read for yourself without any risk of translation errors what it was you had been recorded as saying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but sometimes there may have been some minor mistakes but generally it was okay, some minor mistakes, I'm saying, but generally, it was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think if we look, for example, on page 6 of the statement, in the Albanian original, we can see some minor mistakes that you have corrected as you went through it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the sort of minor mistake that you're referring to where you make a correction and then initial it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes the word was not in the right place, but generally the essence of the text was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we look for example at page 10, again in the Albanian, there is a sentence at the end which you have changed. You see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I deemed it reasonable to do that. That's why I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. No complaint. The short point, Mr. Fazliu, is that you obviously read this statement with care and corrected anything in it that you thought was inaccurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe not 100 per cent, but most of them I found out and corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And was the information that you gave to the Defence investigators on the 15th of June, was that truthful information, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions here in court today as the investigators asked you then, you would give the same answers, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so. Maybe I might not use the same wording, but, of course, I would say the same crux of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then behind tab 3, just so that you can see it, we may or may not need to refer to this, on the 11th of May of this year, you were interviewed by Mr. Di Fazio via videolink in preparation for calling you to give evidence. Do you remember giving an interview to Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours could the witness be asked to wait for the translation of the question before starting the answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, before you answer, could you first wait until Mr. Emmerson has finished because the interpreters, if you start speaking already, they can't interpret the words spoken by two persons simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what you have behind tab 3 is a transcript of that interview. As I say we may or may not need to refer to that. If we can start, please, with tab 1, and with the newspaper article that appears there, I want just to understand the context in a little more detail, if I can, please. Is it the position, Mr. Fazliu, that in March, you became aware for the first time that your name had been included in the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that my name was there, and considered that as deliberate act committed by someone to my detriment or to the detriment of my family. I leave this up to his or her conscience. If I made a statement before, that might have been a momentary statement which shouldn't be taken as a formal statement and not be included in the indictment against someone, but I believe that my name was used deliberately by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, can I stop you there for a moment? Try, if you can, just to focus on the specific question that I'm asking you. I'm not asking you at the moment who it was you think may have used your name, but I think you've confirmed, have you not, that you saw that your name was included within this indictment sometime during March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And prior to that time, had you ever been interviewed by representatives of the Prosecution and given a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I did, but not a statement whereby I accused someone of doing something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can see the text of the newspaper article that appears there and it refers to the 34th point or count on the indictment as it then

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: threatened, and only released when members of your family intervened. Is that correct? That was the allegation in the indictment you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it was in the indictment, and I read it through the Koha Ditore article. It was accusation there, but after that, after hearing a lot of rumours by various individuals, who are meant to utter only bad words, I wanted to make a refutation of the statement and I did that in two or three dailies, I think, Koha Ditore, and some two other newspapers, and that is a text which was written by the office for information in Kline. And I preferred to explain life here whatever I have with respect to this allegation, because kidnap, that word, is not what happened in reality. To be kidnapped is something completely different of what the reality was. And I think I have explained this fact, this action, the kidnapping is like someone throws you a sack over your head, ties your hand or pushes you to some car, it's different when you are just taken to a place, and you just talk freely and are free to do what you -- to say what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause there, Mr. Fazliu, because I'm going to take you through what actually happened in some detail, so if you wait for the question, you'll have an opportunity to explain. Now, the next question I want to ask you is by the time of this newspaper article in March 2005, can I take it by then you were very familiar with the appearance of Mr. Haradinaj? You knew what he looked like by March 2005, presumably from media and newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so, the passage I want to take you to in the English is just below halfway down, which begins on the 24th of May, and in the Albanian of the newspaper article, it is the 4th column, the first full sentence beginning from there. The newspaper article records you as having said, "On the 24th of May, KLA soldiers asked us to go to the headquarters in order to discuss the reorganisation and the defence of the Grabanica village in the municipality of Kline.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Mr. Ramush Haradinaj was not present on that day in the headquarters of Jabllanice, and I have never met him or talked to him." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then leaving the next sentence out, it continues, "After the discussions we had in the headquarters with Mr. Lahi Brahimaj, we agreed that for the time being, with the few weapons we had, we could not defend the village of Grabanica. After this conversation, I left the headquarters without any problems or threats whatsoever, neither from their side nor from my family against the Brahimajs." And again, is that a fair and accurate summary of what you told the reporter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is fully accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't propose, unless Your Honour wishes me to, to go through and read into the record every passage of relevance from the Defence witness statement. The answers that the witness has already given would, on the face of it, meet the requirements of Rule 92 ter, but I don't want to find myself so to speak in the position where the admission of the witness statement is in any way in doubt. So what I would propose to do is to ask the witness some general questions but that on the assumption that the answers that he has already given; namely, that the statement is true and accurate and that he would, if asked the same questions, give the same answers, is sufficient to amount to an adoption of the contents of the statement and to render it admissible. But obviously if Your Honour wishes me to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the statement is here. Tendering it as a Rule 92 ter statement, we have not heard that yet, if you would do that. Of course, when you asked the question on whether the witness would give the same answers, I had at the back of my mind that I recognised those words from Rule 92 ter, so if you want to tender this statement, then we'll hear from --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I had the same thoughts as Your Honours. I assumed that this was coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we are waiting for --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The criteria is fulfilled--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- application to apply under Rule 92 ter for admission of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then formally I do, as I understand Mr. Di Fazio to indicate that the criteria are met, then there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio -- well, of course there are sometimes other matters such as whether there is opinion in there, et cetera et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I haven't looked at it from that perspective. Could I -- as a general principle, yes, I don't have any objections to its admission broadly speaking. There may be excerpts or points in it which I would like to perhaps reserve my position on. Could I have a quick look at it and perhaps let you know by say the second session today if there is any concerns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's a good suggestion. It also allows the Chamber to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if there are any passages upon which it would be necessary for me to further cross-examine on the record, then perhaps Your Honour would be kind enough to give me that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed taking as a starting point that the statement has been tendered as a 92 ter statement and that no objection as yet have been raised. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, before I go to the contents of your statement and the material that is recorded there, you were asked some questions yesterday about why it was, after two days of fighting against the Serb forces in Grabanice, you and your travelling companion did not go immediately that night or in the next two days of your own volition, of your own choice, to Jabllanice in order to discuss a reorganisation of the defences of the village, and you gave certain answers about how late it was and the state of your clothing and so forth. I just want to put those few days into proper perspective for the Chamber. The Serb offensive that you were caught up in on the 19th and 20th of May 1998, how many of the villages in the area around Grabanice were attacked during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This offensive started on the 13th. The Serb forces attacked Kepuz village from Dollove in the early morning hours. At 9.15, we interrupted the lesson in Grabanica and taking the arms, the weapons we had, we started to get ready to defend the village. We reinforced the guards of the village, and part of the population, mainly women and children, left the village, right since that day and found refuge in their relatives in Lugu i Baranit and other villages. On the 16th, when the burial ceremony of -- in Cescko of Caush Morina took place on the 13th, the Serbs maltreated and beat some three, four citizens of Kline. Ahmet Krasniqi, the late Ahmet Krasniqi was one of them. He was chairman of the KLA -- LDK in Kline. And then the Serbs fired in the direction of Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say the Serbs fired, did they have heavy artillery, tanks, and armoured weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had, but on the 16th, they used mortars, sorry, machine-guns, automatic rifles, and shelled the village. They used shelling -- shells. Until the 19th, when Caush got killed. On the 19, Grabanica was attacked at around 6.00 in the afternoon and the attack lasted until 8.00 in the evening, and these created a very bad atmosphere in the village. On the next day, some forces from the KLA came to the village to help us keep our positions, and we managed to keep our positions all day despite the attacks. In the evening of the 20th, all were obliged to withdraw because we ran out of ammunition. This happened after the killing of Faruk Elezi and the wounding of some people who were at these points, among them was also my brother, Aziri. On the 21st, the Serbs entered the village and they set fire to Grabanice and Bokshiq and it was impossible to feel safe and to go back to the village. On the 21st, they killed Sacir Tahiri or Zecir from Bokshiq and an old whose name at this moment, I don't remember. He was from Bokshiq, and then Caush Fazliu was later killed in Bokshiq. So the situation was very desperate. The Serb forces came from Dukagjin [phoen] direction and entered the fields between Bokshiq and Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Brief supplementary questions about this please. First of all, during the attack on the 19th and the 20th, were the Serb forces then using heavy artillery or did they have tanks that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may say that -- I can't give you accurate numbers, but I can tell you that they fired some 300 shells in the course of two hours on the 19th in Grabanice. During the day of the 20th, I couldn't count the weapons they used, armoured cars, machine-guns, all kinds of weapons they used, and a convoy of tanks and armoured cars came from the direction of Peja, another from a direction of Kline, and they came up to the village bridge which is across the first neighbourhood of Granice, which is called Sejdina [phoen] neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The second supplementary question I wanted to ask you is this: By this stage, as I understand your evidence, the women and children had left the village and the men remained behind. Can you give us some idea of the number of men, both villagers and KLA together, who were defending the village against this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that we all together defended the village because there were no uniforms for each and every one, so we were together. We cooperated to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My question was roughly how many men were involved in that process of defending the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there must have been over 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were they all armed or did you have less weapons than men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, 21 or 22 had weapons and two or three had hunting guns. Mainly they had 15 or 17 of them had automatic rifles and three or four had hunting guns. So altogether there were 21 or 22 armed people. There was also a machine-gun station where Faruk Elezi was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, how could the unarmed men come to make a contribution then to defending the village? What was the expectation then in relation to the men without weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were ready and standing by in case someone got killed who had a weapon, they should take that weapon and use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so when the Serbs managed to overrun the village, and you ran out of ammunition, did the men disperse in different directions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th, the Serbs didn't enter the village. This means that they didn't feel safe. They didn't -- they weren't sure that we had left the village. So we didn't withdraw that day. Maybe some did. In the evening of -- in the evening of that day, we withdrew. So the Serbs came into the village on the next day, which is on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And again, so that we are clear because Mr. Di Fazio asked you why you didn't immediately try to organise the village defence on the 21st, did you know where all the other men were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I also said it yesterday in my answer to a question, that personally I had no idea where my wife and my kids were, let alone my brothers, my -- their family members. I only knew that we were at that point. We were six people there. One got wounded. One was in Germany for something, for an affair of his. One went to Jabllanice. So there were only six of us distributed into various points in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the witness statement that I've shown you in tab 2, you don't need to turn it up, but you say that it was on the evening of the next day, the 22nd, that KLA men including "Ujku" or "Wolf" and Nazmi Brahimaj came to the house where you were sheltering, that is Tal Zeka house in Zhabel. So would it be the position that it was within 48 hours of you leaving the village that you had the first discussion with Nazmi Brahimaj about trying to reorganise the village defences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you kindly lead to the page where the -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where in the English translation is page 4 in the final paragraph. And in the Albanian original, it is page 5, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you look at page 5, the second paragraph, you indicate that it was the 22nd of May when you met Ujku with KLA soldiers who entered the house of Tal Zeka and then at the bottom of that page, you describe the conversation that took place with Nazmi Brahimaj about attempts to reorganise the village defences. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So can we take it that it was in fact only 48 hours after you left, evacuated Grabanice after two days of fighting, that you had that first conversation with Nazmi Brahimaj at the house of Tal Zeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may be some minor mistake here with respect to the date. It might have been 23rd, I think, on the first time, and 24th on the second time but I'm repeating it. Everything I had taken down, the notes, but they were destroyed, so. The text is okay. This is the only minor mistake that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The first conversation certainly took place within two or three days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to take this part of the evidence reasonably shortly, but you describe in the statement how Ujku or "Wolf" was insulting on that first night, but you say that he was the only one in the group who was making offensive remarks. And you indicate that the commander from Zhabel, who was there as well, was reprimanding him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. The commander and Nazmi reprimanded him, and then he stopped saying those words because he used these unpleasant words with me and with my companion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So obviously, his behaviour was offensive, but is it right, and I think you used this word when you were interviewed by Mr. Di Fazio earlier on on the videolink, that the others behaved like proper military men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers there who didn't utter a word, whereas this person, as I said, was very offensive. Nothing to do with the proper conduct of a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In particular, the two commanders, that is Tahir from Zhabel and Nazmi from Jabllanice were, in your view, behaving like proper military men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you describe a little further on in the statement a visit that took place the following day, and you've told us about that, in your evidence already, when a group of men came back, including Ujku and Tahir, the commander from Zhabel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it right that again on that occasion, Ujku was offensive but Tahir was not only polite but reprimanded him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And another of those present on that second day was a man called and Arbnori Zeneli who you describe as a very polite man; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For as long as I saw him, during those two contacts in Zhabel and when he took us in his car, I could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you left Tal Zeka's house in Zhabel that day, I think you told us yesterday, and you say so in your statement here as well, that Ujku left the house by vehicle and did not accompany you to Jabllanice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you didn't see him either when you got to Jabllanice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can help us with this, but do you know the real name of Ujku is Pjeter Sala [phoen], or is that something that you're not aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that people addressed him by the name of Ujku and that he had a small beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be absolutely clear, as far as you are concerned, is it correct that you went voluntarily to Jabllanice, having been asked to come together to discuss the reorganisation of the village defences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And nobody forced either you or your travelling companion to go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already started to explain to you earlier on the difference between the word kidnapping and going somewhere on your own free will. Personally speaking, I went there because I wanted to. Nobody forced me to go. We were accompanied by Tahir all the time, and I said it even yesterday, and all along the way, we engaged in private conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If we look in the Albanian at the last paragraph on page 6, and in the English at the second paragraph on page 6, I want to just look at the second sentence with you. You're recorded there as saying this: "We left the village with the group of KLA soldiers, walking to Jabllanice. We did this voluntarily. We were not forced or kidnapped. And there were no acts of violence towards either me or Naser Lika. We all walked together. I walked arm in arm with Tahir from Zhabel, and we had a normal conversation. We discussed my profession and other general things about what we should do about the conflict." Again is that an accurate statement of what took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate. Maybe I haven't been able to put more detail, but they were conversation about the same and the statement would have become longer. But the gist of what happened on the way is correctly reflected on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you describe in the next paragraph how you arrived at Jabllanice, that you went into the HQ building, into a large open, green area at the rear, that you were offered and took some food, that the mood was normal, and that there were some soldiers eating in a big room. You say a few paragraphs further down that there was then a discussion in the room about reorganising village defences, and you say this: "There was no yelling in the room, just a group of men trying to decide what to do and how to do it." Again, is that a fair summary of what took place there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I never heard any screams or shouts apart from the discussions that were taking place or soldiers asking for more tea. That's the only thing which was made -- a request made at a higher tone, but otherwise the rest was normal conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did the discussion end with an agreement that there was insufficient weaponry available to reorganise the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday in my answers there were three reasons, but one of them was more significant than the other two. There was the lack of weaponry, which is the key thing needed for the defence of a village in a wartime. The other thing was -- which was significant, very significant, was that Grabenice and Bokshiq, the two villages, were like an island exposed from three directions to dangers. They were threatened by Serb forces on the eastern side, from Dollova. There was a large number of Serb forces deployed on the side of the main road which was 200, 300 metres from Grabenice, and from another side where the forces were still threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wasn't going to -- I appreciate that you gave that explanation yesterday. I wasn't specifically going to ask to you repeat it. Is there anything you want to add to what you told us yesterday about the reasons or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that if we were to find out where the rest of the family, we had to find that out first, and then we had to keep in touch regarding the remobilisation, when that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you would just like, please, to look at the last paragraph on page 8, if you find page 8 and look at the last paragraph, which for those following the English translation is the first paragraph on page 8. You say there, that during all the time that this was going on, it was daylight. You say you don't know how long you were at the HQ but had arrived in the afternoon and that you knew it was still daylight when you and your travelling companion eventually left. And then you say this: "I think we were the first to leave." Is it your recollection now that you and your travelling companion were the first of the men to leave the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this last paragraph, I hadn't noticed. Something needs to be improved. During all the time it was daylight, I don't know how long we stayed in the village because we arrived afternoon, in the afternoon, and this needs some improvement. I don't know whether anybody else left before, but I think it was me and Naser who were the first, and then we were followed by other people from Grabanice and Bokshiq. Unlike them, we were taken by car to the place we wanted to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask you about that in a moment. You go on to say, "There was no problem with leaving. The discussions were ending and agreements had been made, so my travelling companion and I left." I just want to be absolutely clear, you left the building in company with your travelling companion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then is it right that Arbnori Zeleni, the man you earlier described as having been polite, offered to drive you both wherever you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did your travelling companion wish to go to the house of Haxhi Bajrami on the outskirts of Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was no choice. I think he knew them before I did. He knew their family before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were there other refugees staying at Haxhi Bajrami's house as far as you could see when you got there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you please elicit an answer to the previous question from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me just take this in stages. First of all, did Arbnori Zeleni drive you and your travelling companion to the house of Haxhi Bajrami?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he drove us right up to the door step of Haxhi Bajrami's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And is Haxhi Bajrami's house on the outskirts of Jabllanice or was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's at the entrance of Jabllanice when you come from Gllogjan, and he had houses on both sides of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose idea was it to go to Haxhi Bajrami's house? Was that your idea or was it your travelling companion's idea to go to that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it was and Arbnori who suggested that there was someone from my family who was staying at Haxhi Bajrami's house and that's how it turned out to be. And that's how we decided to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you got there, were there other refugees staying there in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were other refugees, mainly relatives of the Bajrami family.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you then leave Haxhi Bajrami's house that same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening of that day, I left and went to Maznik, to the family of Abdisula [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did your travelling companion remain behind at Haxhi Bajrami's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he stayed there, but I don't know where he went on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he still there when you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us some indication or estimate of what time it was by the time you left or is that not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said I did not have a watch on me, so it's just a guess. It's going to be a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I wonder if I may, please, to ask you to go to back to page 8 of your witness statement and to look at the second full paragraph, that is the large paragraph in the centre of the page, and in the English translation that is the last paragraph on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: remained together during all of the events I have described above. He stayed with me as we walked, ate, and discussed things." The question I want to ask you is this: Was your travelling companion in your company, that is to say with you, from the time that you arrived in the village of Jabllanice that day until the time you left him at Haxhi Bajrami's house? Were you together throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There has been some confusion here. We were not together in the house of Haxhi Bajrami. We were together up until the moment that we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you again then. Were you together with your travelling companion between the time you arrived in the village of Jabllanice that day and the time when you arrived at the house of Haxhi Bajrami? Were you together throughout the events of that afternoon and evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely so. We were together all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I have two further questions, then, if I may, please. Just bear with me for one second. If you could look at page 9 in the Albanian version of the statement, and at the second-to-last paragraph on that page, which in the English translation is page 8, in the penultimate paragraph, it reads as follows: "I have been asked if I saw any rough or ill treatment of people whilst I was at Jabllanice HQ, and I have been asked if I saw a young boy having his ear cut off. Neither of these incidents happened whilst I was at the Jabllanice HQ with my travelling companion. I never saw anyone touched or beaten, and I never heard anything like that occurring." Is that the truth, Mr. Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question. If you say, "I never heard," that goes until when? Did you up until today never hear about such things or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the text, and I am saying about whilst I was there, I never heard anything of what is described in the text. So nobody being beaten or no one being having his ear chopped on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's what you heard at that time. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The very last question that I want to ask you, Mr. Fazliu, relates to page 8 of your statement, and to the second paragraph, which on the English translation is the second paragraph on page 7, which reads, "I do know 100 per cent that Ramush Haradinaj was not present on that day. I must add that I would not have recognised him on that day as I did not know him then but I have seen him since on the TV, and I do know that he was not present on that day in the Jabllanice HQ." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is more than accurate, and I'm fully convinced that he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please just for the assistance of Defence counsel, can I just indicate that I've got no objection to the statement going fully into evidence in its entirely under the provisions of Rule 93 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is on the record. The Chamber will decide on the matter but of course, since we have not studied this document before, we'll need a bit of time as well to read it. Mr. Guy-Smith, any questions in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I maintain the position that I took yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, Mr. Harvey, I take it that you would like to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Fazliu, Mr. Harvey is counsel for Mr. Brahimaj. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fazliu. I'd like to ask you a few questions first in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, just, you are aware that we returned into open session. You're also aware of the public-private policy in this case developed by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you'll keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very much so. I know it's been a while since I've been on my feet, but I haven't completely forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions in relation to Jabllanice. I think you've indicated before that Jabllanice was even as early as 1992, 1993, under fairly constant surveillance by the Serb authorities and that people of Jabllanice were under constant risk of attack at that time. Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the surveillance is concerned, it may not be compliant with the reality, but it was their intention to find an excuse to get into Jabllanice but they did not achieve this until the middle of the war because the inhabitants of Jabllanice managed to disarm some policemen, Serb policemen, and they never managed to get into Jabllanice. For them, Jabllanice; for the Serbs, Jabllanice, was something which they couldn't occupy for about six years, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you refer to the middle of the war, you're talking about 1998. Do you recall when the Serbs first attacked Jabllanice in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may say that on several occasions, they shelled Jabllanice but the first offensive, it was at the beginning of July, if I'm not mistaken, and that is in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You had discussions earlier in 1998, you went, I believe, with Enver Berisha, to meet with some of the KLA in Jabllanice and you met then with Myrte Zeneli; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was Myrte. There was a man by the name of Rexhep, but there were some others whose names I have forgotten. It was planned for Lahi to be present at that meeting, but we were told that he had an important mission to attend to and he couldn't be present. We stayed there very late after midnight, it was 1.00 or 2.00 after midnight but it's a long --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall in which month that meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of March, sometime around about that time, which is after the attacks on the family of Adem Jashari in Prekaz and after the attacks in Cheraz [phoen] and Liksen [phoen]. It was between the 5th and the 10th, but it was the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And at that time, was there great concern in your village and in Jabllanice that you too might come under attack from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was no village who was not concerned about a possible attack by the Serb forces because during the day, the Serb forces were patrolling the area, although during the night, the patrols were less frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At that stage, if I understand your evidence correctly, sir, there was no KLA organisation in your village, as such, you just had a number of members of the LDK who had formed a defence group to protect your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting, but I take that answer to mean at that stage, when my learned colleague asked at that stage, he was talking about March I assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, and now I'm going to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting that we leave the topic, all I wanted to be clear was -- [Speakers overlapping]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to be clear what at that stage meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, let me just make clear, at that stage we are talking about March through April of 1998, again there was no KLA organisation as such in your village, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During March, I may say that there was no, or at least I wasn't aware, of any KLA presence, and it may be said of April I cannot say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When did Sadri Berisha first become a member of the KLA in your village, as far as you're aware, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I Can't remember the date. I can't remember the date. But I -- I recall that it -- 13th of May 1998. After the first attacks by the Serb forces in the villages including Qeskove.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When your village defence, when your village needed defending after the 13th of May, you had assistance from the villagers in Jabllanice, I think you've said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were KLA soldiers also from Jabllanice. There were some two or three from Mitrovica who came to help in Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Can you help the Tribunal with how this happened. I can put two alternatives to you, and maybe there is a third, but perhaps you would just like to help us with how this came about. Was it that there was a KLA command telling you: This is what you've got to do, we're going to take charge here, all of you do as we say? Or was it you in Grabanice putting out a call, anyone who has got a gun, please come and help us? Can you give the Tribunal a sense of how organised this was or whether it was just really a question of people getting together to try and help each other out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must take more time to explain this. Starting from 1991, since 1991, my elder brother managed to secure some 12 automatic weapons and they were bought between 2.800 to 3.500 deutschmarks, and they were distributed among members of families which were more secure, from our point of view, to look after these weapons. And from then onwards, we organised our village defences up until 1998, and from 1998, as I said yesterday, there were two groups within a period of 10 days or two weeks, they went from -- left Grabanice to go to Albania to bring weapons back and that was done in coordination with the KLA headquarters in Jabllanice. Part of those weapons were given out to soldiers of -- KLA soldiers in Kepuz, in Cermjan, and that was used for reinforcing those points, and that happened just before and up until the moment that the front was opened in Grabanice too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My question, sir, was more along the lines of did you consider yourselves under orders from the KLA or just working in cooperation with other members of the KLA who were in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must explain that. Those six soldiers who stayed with us for three, four days, and they stayed in my house, in the oda of men, it was me personally who sewed the KLA emblems on their caps. And if the otherwise was true, I don't know how I would have said that, but for me there was no problem in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not making myself clear, but let's put it this way: Was there any tension between LDK and KLA or did you all get along fine together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was coordinated between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There was no hostility between the people of Grabanice and the people of Jabllanice between LDK and KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have been people like Ujku, for example, but otherwise, on the whole, it was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Also we know at some point that the -- there were Serbs in Grabanice who chose to leave the village. Was pressure put on them to leave, or did they leave of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must explain here that from Grabanice, no one pushed the Serbs out of the village. One single family, the Rajlovic family, they lived in Bokshiq, they left voluntarily, and they passed through Grabanice. Nobody caused any problems to them. In fact, the KLA soldiers accompanied, escorted them, and they did not create any problems for them. They had one or two children with them. They had a family member who was a policeman. And no problems were created for them. They were escorted through the village, out of the village, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. I don't know when you want to take the break. This would be a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's usually after one hour and a half, but we started a little bit over quarter past 2. If this is a suitable moment for you, it's fine as far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, there was a mill in Grabanice, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is even now there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that mill back in 1998 serviced a lot of villages in the surrounding area, people came from different villages to have their corn ground up at the mill in Grabanice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's been offering its services until the outbreak of the war in Grabanice. Then it was -- it didn't operate during the wartime and then after the war, it was reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So the mill shut down. Was that because the electricity supply was cut off or because it was just not safe to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, but mostly because of lack of electricity. We didn't a power generator at that time, so we had to interrupt work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was there just the one mill or more than one mill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some other family had its own mill, but this mill we had serviced many other people. The entire locality, I would say. Whoever wanted to have its corn ground brought it there or to turn the corn into fodder for the animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say the mill shut down at the outbreak of the war, can you put an approximate date on that? Was that as early as the attack on Kapuz on the 13th of May or later or before then, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, upon the attack against Kapuz and Ceskove the mill shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Again, you put that at the 13th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, around that date

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to come to the time when you were walking together with your travelling companion from Grabanice and you met Mr. Lahi Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, we have dealt with those portions of the -- I would say the journey in private session until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm about to ask that we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I anticipated that you would like to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session? 7 [Private session][Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Trial Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You I think told us that your brother had been wounded on the 21st of May. Is that your brother Hazir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wounded on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. He was taken after he was wounded to Jabllanice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And he was taken to the clinic or ambulance that was in the house of Myftari Brahimaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know to whose house he was taken. I only know that it was a make-shift hospital in Jabllanice where all wounded were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Also, there was a man called Vesel Berisha, who was very badly wounded in Grabanice; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was wounded too but he was wounded as a result of a shell in the street, a little far away from our home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And do you recall that he was taken initially to Jabllanice but that his injuries were so serious that he had to be transported to Irzniq to the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that. I heard that his life was this in peril because he was gravely wounded. To this day he's suffering from that wound as a result of that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's in connection that I want to ask you -- in connection with that that I want to ask you about your meeting with Lahi Brahimaj on the road. You've told us that Lahi was leaving Jabllanice and driving in the direction of Gllogjan and Peja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't said that he was -- he set out in the direction of Gllogjan. I only said that he was in a car, in a vehicle, together with another soldier, and that he stopped the car and he greeted us quite normally, and sincerely, and that he asked us where we were going and that we told him, and that he asked us if we could hand over the weapon because he said, "We are short of weapons in the front line." So he kindly asked us to surrender the automatic rifle, which I did, and then I asked him, that when I needed the weapon he should bring it back to me, and this is what happened. My companion also handed over two hand grenades he had on him. I didn't know he had them in his possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you about, let's see if you remember this or not, do you recall that there were two vehicles; that Lahi was in a jeep and that in fact, Vesel Berisha was being carried in the vehicle in front? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, I saw that he was in one car, and I saw only one car. He was with another friend. I didn't see any other vehicle, at least not at the moment that we had that conversation with him and then we went on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You, in Tal's house, you were staying in his oda with the rest of the men, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were staying in the men's oda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you were there for a total of three days approximately; is that right, two to three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And during that time did you simply stay in that one room the whole time, or did you mover around Tal's farm and premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in the oda, in the room, during all the time, even though I had offered my services to the owner. I had offered to help him if he needed us because it was a spring time and he might need our help, but he insisted that we stay in that room all the time, and this is what we did, myself, my travelling companion, and some other persons who were sheltering there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when the soldiers, the KLA soldiers, came from Jabllanice and from Zhabel, they talked to all of you men who were there, who had been involved in the defence of Grabanice, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't talk with all of them. Because the first time they stayed very briefly, a total of ten minutes. I don't think it was longer than that, and it was some brief conversations that took place during those ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And the second time, did they talk with more of the men who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time when Ujku came to the antechamber of that room, it was only myself and my travelling companion present in the room. Some others were downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Coming back to your travelling companion, you recall that you were asked -- you had a conversation by videolink with Mr. Di Fazio from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th of May this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And do you recall telling him that the last time you had seen your travelling companion was about two years ago or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may say now that maybe it was three years ago when I saw him last. Even the first time I said around two years, but now I may say that it was three years ago that I saw him for the first time, and I have no clue as to where he is. Before he left the village, he used to say that I will go to America. This is something that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at page, for those who are following the transcript, that we have at page 37, at the answers that you gave to Mr. Di Fazio there, and it's at the bottom two-thirds of the way down, and Mr. Di Fazio was asking you about the big lie that Naser -- that your travelling companion had been telling. You recall him asking you about the big lie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish to speculate. I don't want to insult anyone. I never heard of anyone else, but based on the question posed of me by Mr. Di Fazio, I came to the conclusion that when I was asked, the moment that I personally left the headquarters of KLA in Jabllanice, whether Naser was left behind, I thought that this was a big lie because both of us left at the same time and that Naser didn't remain behind, and I still abide by this. It's not true that Naser remained behind. Both of us left at the same time and got into Arbnori's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The part of the conversation with Mr. Di Fazio that I wanted to draw to your attention was where you told him this: "The main thing he was talking about was how to get abroad, how to get documents, and things about that nature." Was that something that Naser seemed -- sorry, your travelling companion seemed to be very concerned about, he wanted to find some way to get documents so that he could travel abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war, with his first wife, he had an opportunity, because I had some connections with some relief organisations, contributing to the reconstruction of schools, and I contacted a person called Paula [phoen]. She managed to send his first wife to Italy for treatment, but she died, unfortunately, his first wife. He remarried and then he worked for a while in Peja. I'm not sure whether he worked for KFOR or I don't know. And then all the time he kept saying that I'm trying to get my papers in order to go somewhere abroad, in America or elsewhere. That was what I heard from him until the last moment that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Di Fazio, to re-examine the witness, I would like to ask two additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, earlier today you said, and I'll just try to find that, you said in relation to the comments you made in the dailies, you said, "If I made a statement before, that might have been a momentary statement which shouldn't be taken as a formal statement and not be included in the indictment against someone." Now, did you give any statement to anyone prior to the learning about the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that if I have given a statement, because to tell you the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is: Did you give a statement, not commenting on if you would have given a statement, but I'd like to know whether you gave a statement before March 2005. And if so, to whom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have anyone to give a statement to other than the people I gave the statement in Vienna [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us. I've got no idea about any statement earlier to March 2005. Could you please tell us to whom did you give a statement? And as you said, in Vienna? The Chamber is not aware of any earlier statement than October 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm repeating it. I don't remember. That's why I allowed for this if I -- I said if I gave a statement, I did not intend to accuse anyone by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is, and since you just referred apparently to a place even where you would have given a statement, if I understood you well, you said "other than the people I gave the statement in Vienna." Did you give a statement, whether in Vienna or elsewhere, before the -- before March 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: He said a word in Albanian meaning later which sounds like Vienna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I didn't given any statement in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That now has been corrected. The interpreters had heard a word and -- but forget about Vienna. Did you give to anyone a statement in relation to what you, in March 2005, considered to be wrong in the indictment? Did you give a statement to anyone? Whether humanitarian organisation, whether investigators, whether whomever, so before you learned about the indictment to which you commented, did you give a statement to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that after explaining the situation in the media, then I gave statements, but not before. I don't remember to have given any statements before the explanation I gave to the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you said, "If I made a statement before, that might have been a momentary statement which shouldn't be taken as a formal statement and not be included in the indictment against someone," which at least suggests that you considered it a possibility that you had given a statement which was then abused for purposes of drafting an indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I thought. If I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just crossed my mind as the interchange between Your Honour and the witness was taking place that the word "statement" is capable potentially of two meanings, a written document or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that and therefore I used the same word for the witness. That's -- otherwise I would have asked him whether he ever signed a written statement. But that answer is -- Now, another matter, Mr. Fazliu, I'd like to ask you a question about. You said you were willing to help when you were in the village of -- let me just find it -- when you were in the house of Tal Zeka at Zhabel. You said you were quite willing to give him a hand, to help him, but he insisted on you staying in the men's oda all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why was that? I mean, it was May. Staying for a couple of days in exactly that same place, not leaving it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably he didn't want me to help him because that was the first time I was visiting him and that I was, as I said, wearing just an old T-shirt, and that there were other people there that he allowed to help him in his field work, but he didn't want a guest like me staying with him for two, three days to go out and help him work in the fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now even -- it's not only that he did not, as you told us, that he didn't want you to help him, but also that he insisted that you should stay in the oda. Of course you could leave that for other purposes than just to help Mr. Tal Zeka. Did he allow you to leave the oda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we wanted we could have left, but as my personal situation is dressed as I was, I wouldn't venture to leave the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the others could freely leave the oda or those who were with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two or three neighbours of ours who are related to Tal. They were -- they left. Bajram Lika was his name and his sons, they left the house freely and came back. He could come and go like he was in his own house; whereas myself, and my companion, we remained during all the time in the oda, in the room, for two days because I'm not counting the nights because, as you know, during the night one rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were the only two who stayed in the room, is that correctly understood, for these days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two other persons -- two or three other persons from Turjake who met with some acquaintance of theirs, Dzevad was there with a brother of his. They met and talked together. They stayed for half an hour or one hour, and then they went back. Then there was Bajram and his sons who could leave and come, and a relative of his who, as I said, were free to move about Tal's family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question here, in your response you more or less tell who visited others who were in the room. My question was whether you and your travelling companion were the only ones who stayed as long as you were in this house in this room for all the time or whether there were others as well who stayed for these two or three days inside the men's oda, inside that room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only me, myself, and my companion, remained in the room all the time, with exception of some personal needs, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Earlier today, you testified "he," and you were referring to the owner of the house, "he insisted that we stay in that room all the time and this is what we did, myself, my travelling companion, and some other persons who were sheltering there." So earlier today you said that not just you and your travelling companion but others stayed in the room for all this time as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that he insisted, but he said, "You don't need to work, because you are guests here." As to the presence of other people, there were other people who stayed two, three hours, then they left and went to visit Tal's brothers or to other families in the village. But it was only myself and my companion who remained there all the time, without moving, without leaving the room for a long -- for long stretches of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question is about Ujku. I think it was Defence counsel who asked you whether you knew the name of the person called Ujku. Did you have no knowledge of either first name or family name at the time when he -- when you met him in -- I always forget this -- in Zhabel, did you have any knowledge of his first name or family name apart from that he was called Ujku.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I didn't know his name. I only knew him by the pseudonym Ujku. But later on, through the media and the writings, I may have heard, and I think I've seen a name which coincides with the name given to him, but at the time I did not know who that person's real name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember what media? Was that television, newspapers? Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the press. I cannot say precisely now which of the newspapers, whether it was Bota Sot or Koha Ditore. In one of these newspapers, there was a name which could be the real name of the person that was also known as Ujku.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember what name was published then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Pjeter, but again I'm saying I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did you learn this from the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was after the indictment was issued against the former Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio? Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I've still got some questions I'd like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just on the question of work for the man, Tal Zeka, the work that you had in mind when you offered to help him out, was that properly described as heavy work, perhaps work in the fields, with the crops, that sort of work? Is that the work you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I told him that if you need any help, we can help you rather than sit idle. It could be something -- some work in agriculture like planting peppers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I thought you meant. Thank you for that clarification. I appreciate it. And did you offer that when you arrived at the house or at least the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we arrived it was night-time. I cannot exactly say what time it was, but it was the following day after we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So you felt quite able to, notwithstanding the states of your clothes, to go out into the fields and do some agricultural work? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with those clothes that we had on, we could use them because they were suitable for doing work, and obviously they were good for doing some work, but if I was to go in those clothes for a visit to somebody, I would like ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were -- it was fine for the agricultural work around the oda and in the presence of all the others people who were gathered in the oda or the other families, it was okay for those purposes, your clothing, do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the oda they were not quite appropriate, but they did not have other options, and I didn't have other options, and in the circumstances I had to do with what I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll perhaps move on. You have revealed to us today, you have a statement you provided in June of 2006, and I'd like you to just ask you a few questions about that. You say in that statement that you've had the opportunity of having your ICTY statement read over to you, and you wanted to make some comments in relation to the content. Now, do you recall saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which statement are you talking about? Can you please repeat that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. Sure. I'll be clear. I just wanted to remind you that in your statement that you gave, not entirely clear to me at this stage who to, but in any event the statement that you gave on the 15th of June 2006, and which you signed and which Mr. Emmerson showed you earlier today, in that statement, I think you've got it right in front of you there, yes, in that statement you say that you had your ICTY statement read over to you in your native language, and you then go on to make some comments, some clarifications. Do you see that in your statement? If I may help you, it's the fourth paragraph of your statement shown to you by Mr. Emmerson today, the one dated 15 June 2006 that you have right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please give me details on which pages that they are on and which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on this. It's the fourth paragraph of your statement dated 15 June 2006. It was shown to you a matter of an hour and a half or so ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio it seems to be the first paragraph on page 2 in the language --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, probably page 2, sorry. Unfortunately they haven't got numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind you, Mr. Fazliu, that you said that you had your -- the ICTY statement that you gave read over to you and that you then go on to say that you want to make some comments and clarifications or comments. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. And you remember, don't you, the statement being shown to you and read over to you by the person who took this statement from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to be absolutely clear that you were talking about the same statement. So could the witness be shown 65 ter 1919, and I'd like him to be shown the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our information, is that the 11th of October, 2005 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not in the binder. Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's on the screen both English and Albanian available on the screen, and could I ask that we scroll down to the bottom of that page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that your signature that appears at the bottom of your page -- that page, Mr. Fazliu? I'll repeat my question. Is that your signature that appears at the bottom of that page, Mr. Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I ask the Court, please, to go through to the very last page of the statement. And does your signature appear again on this last page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that is the statement that you're referring to when you say that you provide some clarifications in your statement that you gave in June of 2006, correct? That's the ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, listening at the line of questioning, I don't know whether this also should be in private session because we still are. Whenever we were talking about journey, companion, et cetera, but unless what you are aiming at comes down to the same episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't intend to show content of the statement on the screens if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not just a matter of the screen. That's not what I'm concerned about, but whether this portion of the evidence should be in private session at all because we limit private session more or less to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes -- no, no. I think we can go out of private session. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We then turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honours for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You've very helpfully provided some clarifications in your statement of June of 2006, but the ICTY statement that we have up on the screen here, and if we just scroll down on that last page, please, or, rather, scroll up slightly, it's in English, but that's an acknowledgement that the apparently signed by you, that the statement was read over to you in the Albanian language and was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection and that you gave it voluntarily. Can you tell us if, when you gave your ICTY statement, if it was read over to you by an interpreter in the Albanian language? Can you recall that happening at the time that you put your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that the interpreter said that we will bring you a copy in the Albanian language. I can't remember whether it was read out to me in Albanian. I have said it in the statement that I've given to you, that some interpreters, they come from Albania, and they have difficulties in understanding some of the expressions that we use and there have been -- there has been confusion over certain sentences or ideas that have been said in interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So I just want to be clear about that. Are you saying that you can't remember if your ICTY statement was interpreted to you? You can't recall if that happened or not, when you signed it, when you put your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I signed it, I signed it in [indiscernible] language. And if it was translated to me, there have been mistakes made in that translation, when the translation of certain words and expressions.
