And I have also made some corrections in the statement given to Defence. I have made certain corrections, but there haven't been as many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'd like to have matters clear. Was, when you signed this statement, was it translated to you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I have not seen a copy of the statement translated into Albanian, I have not considered it as translated, but probably it was my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I'm not asking what you considered or what your interpretation of the situation was. I simply asked you when you signed this statement, English statement, was it read to you through translation in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said earlier, I cannot remember that such a thing happened, whether such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you have considered it a possibility that you would sign a statement in a foreign language without knowing what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said, we trust people and sometimes if you -- if you trust people, then sometimes it gets you on the wrong path. And I would normally trust people there. But now I notice that there are certain mistakes in that statement which do not coincide with the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know, Mr. Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because on the basis of the questions that I received via the videolink, I noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was that the videolink that you had with me earlier this year? My question was: You noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise for rising. I wonder if the witness might remove his ear phones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please remove your ear phones for a second, Mr. Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm slightly anxious that there is a risk that the way in which the witness is being questioned about this has the potential for confusing him, because Mr. Di Fazio began his re-examination by directing the witness's attention to the passage in his Defence statement in which he says in terms and which he confirmed, that whilst the Defence statement was being taken, the ICTY statement was read over to him in Albanian so that he was then able to identify errors that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although -- yes. That's.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour asked him the question: "How do you know, Mr. Fazliu?" He's already answered the question in the sense that he began in answering to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes he asked the same thing in two different ways in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My concern is that the way in which this is being done has the potential to confuse the witness when he's already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll keep a close eye on that. Mr. Di Fazio, could you please proceed? Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll ask it in the most direct fashion. When did you first become aware of your ICTY statement requiring clarifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was when Defence approached me and through the interview that we had together later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. And could you tell the Trial Chamber how it was that these -- this requirement for clarifications was -- how you became aware of this requirement for clarifications when defence approached you, what precisely happened, how it happened when you became aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I believe that the manner of the question as posed has a sufficient line of ambiguity that the translation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is granted. Could you -- "How you become aware of this requirement" is rather vague and could easily create confusion, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you approached by some individual on behalf of the Defence and questioned about your ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Any time. I don't know when this happened. If it happened. I'm just asking you this: Were you approached by some individual on behalf of the Defence and questioned about the content of your ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only statement is the one that is in front of me and that's the only statement I've given to Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, I'd like to ask you some questions about the content of your ICTY statement because you go into it in some detail in your statement that you gave to Defence. You said that the quote from your ICTY statement; namely, "If Ramush Haradinaj or his people came to know of my statements to The Hague Tribunal I will fall from grace in the eyes of the public and they will start treating me as a traitor, I have never met nor spoken with Ramush Haradinaj, I have only heard of him through Radio and news coverage of his actions, it would be totally illogical for me to be afraid of him. "I wish to say that I never said these things. I have never had any problems with either Ramush Haradinaj or any of his supporters. I am not in fear of him." So you -- can I ask you this: When you spoke to the people from the ICTY and you provided that ICTY statement, did you even go to the topic of whether or not -- of the attitude that Ramush Haradinaj might have to your provision of a statement, to your giving a statement? Did you even discuss that with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I considered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. My question is this: Did you ever discuss the topic at all, even discuss it, with investigators from the OTP, namely, the topic of Ramush Haradinaj or his people coming to know of your statement and you falling from grace in the eyes of the public? Did that topic ever arise in the course of your dealings with OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to clarify once again that during the translation of the statement, there may have been mistakes made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I'm going to stop you there. I'd like you to answer the question of Mr. Di Fazio. The question simply was whether, during the interview, the matter of how your statement would appreciated by Mr. Haradinaj or his people was raised at all, yes or no. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I haven't talked about this. This was -- this was a conversation which has come out through the clarification that I issued through the statement as well as through the article published in Bota Sot. Up until the end of the war, I had never met or known or spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, again you seem to misunderstand my question. You can form an opinion on how your statement will be appreciated by Mr. X, Y or Z, without knowing that person. I'm not asking for logic. Simply, was the matter, whether people would dislike your statement or even the fact that you gave a statement, if they would become aware, was -- has that been part of your conversation with the investigator of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, look, you can never stop people from speculating and making rumours, but when the name -- my name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about speculations, I'm not talking about rumours. I would like to have a clear answer to the question whether this matter, that is how people might appreciate your statement, was part of the conversation you had with the investigators, which means whether you spoke about this subject when interviewed with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember having discussed this with them, but it may have been probably a question put, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have translated where you said, "I don't remember having discussed this with them, but it may have been probably a question put" and then the translation stops for us. Could you therefore resume your answer from, "But I may have -- it may have been probably a question put". Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it may have been a question put to me by the people who were asking me to give a statement. It may have been an interpreter or an investigator. And it may have been interpreted as if I said it. But I don't remember saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand your answer well that it is that others would perhaps have said that your statement or the content of it would not be positively appreciated, but where these words in the report are yours, that, as a matter of fact, the interpreters or the interviewers might have said it but not you? Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the statement [No interpretation] I cannot conclude that it was put by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, when you learnt from the Defence representative that these words, "If Ramush Haradinaj or his people come to know of my statement to The Hague Tribunal, I will fall from grace in the eyes of the public and they will start treating me as a traitor," when you learned that those words had been attributed to you in your ICTY statement, what was your reaction? Did you -- how did you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made that clarification in the statement given to Defence, and this is included here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I know and I'm very grateful to you for explaining that to us, but what I'm asking you is how did you feel about that? Were you annoyed or upset about these words that had been incorrectly attributed to you? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people here, Mr. Emmerson and the interpreter, Isak by name, they know very well whether I was concerned, really worried about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, again, would you please answer the questions? The question is not what others think your mood was at the time, but the question was whether you -- how you felt about it, whether you were annoyed or upset. Would you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For something I do not have, of course I have to be -- to feel annoyed or upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you consider doing anything about that? For example, speaking to the investigators who had attributed, falsely or incorrectly at least, attributed these words to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the statement I gave to the Defence, you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Again, a very simple question. When you found out, when you found out that these words had been attributed to you concerning Ramush Haradinaj and his people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I think the witness sought confirmation of that moment to be after he gave the statement to the Defence, and I think he earlier said that at that moment he became aware of the incorrect content of the statement. So therefore, yes, Mr. Fazliu, I think that's what Mr. Di Fazio meant, whether -- whether you considered doing anything about it, about this, after you had learned about the incorrectness of the statement as it was put on paper. For example, addressing the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, and could the witness take off his ear phones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why he could not first answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm objecting to the relevance of the question and I think the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's relevance then it's -- then it doesn't -- the worst that it could happen is that it doesn't harm. Five seconds. It won't take more time. Would you please answer the question, whether you considered to do anything about it, to address the investigators who did write down your statement so incorrectly on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the statement I gave to the Defence, I did this. So I did declare what I feel and think and that is the reality. It's quoted well here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about another paragraph in your statement, and in fact, it's -- I just want to focus on paragraph 17 of the -- of your -- of the statement that you gave to the ICTY, and which you've today provided clarification about, and that's the statement -- if we could just look at that particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours I think we might need to go into private session here because it might be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 17 of the statement, yes, if the witness could have the Albanian, that would be -- the Albanian version I understand that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- the Court can have the English as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have the English in front of me. I would very much like to see the Albanian as a matter of fact, whether it's signed or not, because you earlier showed him the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I believe it -- can we scroll down to the bottom, please? No. It's just a straight translation, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without any -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, there is paragraph 17 of the ICTY statement. And today you have provided some clarification about that statement that you gave in the past. And today you have said that you saw this paragraph in which you say -- which you alleged to have said that you saw Lahi Brahimaj in Gllogjan and that he instructed the villagers not to assist villagers from Grabanice as he considered you traitors, and today you've clarified that you didn't make this comment, it's not true, you didn't see or talk to him in Gllogjan. There's just one extra question I want to ask you about. Did Lahi Brahimaj ever exhort or encourage villagers from anywhere not to assist you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not encourage them not to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he did not want to, he would not be sending him -- my brother-- to be cured --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His brother, sorry, to be cured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to ask you a similar question as I asked you in relation to the other matter in your statement. When you found out that this had been included in your statement, your ICTY statement, the one that you signed -- Let me withdraw that. Did you ever discuss with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, as there was just a pause there, there appeared to be a little confusion about what was meant by "otherwise he would not have sent my brother to be cured, his brother to be cured." Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I did read your mind earlier, you read my mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You explained, Mr. Fazliu, you said, and you were talking about Lahi Brahimaj, "He did not encourage them not to help us." And then you explained that, and it had got something to do with a brother being cured. But that is perhaps due to a translation error but that's not entirely clear. Could you please explain again why you thought that he would not encourage them not to help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying again, maybe it's not good to confuse things with a statement of someone else maybe. Lahi has helped both the villagers and that's why I said that the brother was sent to be cured and Sadri Berisha and all the others who were there were sent to Irzniq hospital, and I said this was to prove that he did not stop or prevent anyone else from helping us. Otherwise, if something like that were to occur, I -- there -- I would not give him my machine-gun and then ask it to be brought back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say, "why I said that the brother was sent to be cured," whose brother were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My brother who was wounded in Grabanice. He was sent to be cured and he was treated in Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was the topic of Lahi Brahimaj instructing villagers not to assist you because you were traitors ever discussed with OTP investigators? I'm not asking you if it's true or not. I'm not asking you that. I'm just asking you was the topic ever discussed with OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that it was discussed. And I have clarified this in the statement that I gave to you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And again, when the Defence representatives pointed this out to you, that these words had been attributed to you in your ICTY statement, how did you feel about that? What was your reaction? Did you feel that you had been tricked or were you angry or upset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't feel that was honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Well, I want to leave the topic of your statement. You've given evidence today about a number of matters. I just want to remind you very briefly about them. You agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, leaving the statement, are we entering into the journey or -- I'm just cautious about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think we can go back into open session. I'm not going to go into the journey or the individual that we are all concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Oh, no, first let's turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've said you provided us with clarifications about a number of issues today in your evidence, Mr. Fazliu. You told us that Jabllanice was an area that Serbs couldn't go to for a period of six years and that was still the case, wasn't it, in May of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And not only that, but you had received assistance from people in Jabllanice in your resistance to the Serbs prior to going to Zhabel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were Agim Zeneli and some people who knew Agim, I knew Agim personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you said today that there was, as far as you could detect, no hostility between people from Grabanica and the KLA. I think you described your relationships as "okay." That's your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Grabanice did send help in foods and in fuel to Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And your brother was wounded and taken to Jablanica for medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And this was before you started out on your trip to Zhabel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day of 20th of May, he was wounded, and during the day, he was sent, and then we went late in the evening to Zhabel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And when you set out for Zhabel you knew your brother had been taken to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned later that my brother is being treated because of the wounds he has -- he had taken in the Jablanica HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm looking at the map. I don't need to show it to you, I don't think, unless you wish to see it, you please let me know if you wish. But if you travel from Grabanica in the direction of Zhabel, you first -- you would go through Bokshiq, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then you would go through Glodjane and Peja, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then you'd go through Jablanica, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jabllanice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then in order to get to Zhabel, you'd have to travel on from Jablanica down to Zhabel, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, given the state of your relations with Jablanica and in the light of your evidence, what it was precisely that caused you to keep moving and not stop in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know well that Jabllanice was overburdened with villagers from Grabanice and Bokshiq, because everyone believed it's an area that has been for six years safe because Serbs haven't been there for six years, and I'm not going to call them refugees, but that's why most of people decided to go to a less-burdened village, and in the Beranj area villages it was not very safe because the military forces, Serbian military forces, could have gone any time to beat up the people and even kill them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As you travelled and walked along and your journey towards Zhabel with your travelling companion, did you consider or discuss between the two of you taking refuge in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Grabanice, when we set off, and passed through Bokshiq, we saw people walking on the streets, and he said, "I have a relative in Zhabel and we can go there." I did not know at that time who it was, but after we went I learned this was Tal. And then I had known him earlier a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So then your travelling companion, then, he was clear that he wanted to go to Zhabel? Do I understand your evidence correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear to him where he was going. If it were earlier, maybe I would go to Dasinovac where I have my relatives, and would have been maybe freer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. As you went through Jablanica with your travelling companion, you say there were other villagers from Grabanica there. About how many would you say were there, as you walked through Jablanica or passed through it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never thought of counting them. There were tens of the people. Someone in tractors, someone else walking, some people even with their cars, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But the topic of perhaps abandoning Zhabel and staying in Jablanica never arose between you and your travelling companion? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not really get the question, please. Can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've told us a lot of details about your trip with your travelling companion from Grabanica to Zhabel and reasons why you went there. You've told us a lot about your relations with people in Jablanica and the situation in Jablanica today. All I want to know is this: Did the topic of taking refuge in Jablanica, as you passed through Jablanica, arise between you and your travelling companion? Did you discuss it, something along the lines, for instance, of, "Let's stay here in Jablanica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primary aim of my companion was to learn first where his wife and children are. I believe this is -- was -- this was his primary cause, because he exchanged a couple of words with Ujku related to this issue, and this, I believe, was his primary aim, to learn where his family had sought refuge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm looking at the clock and I wonder whether you'll finish in one or two minutes. If not then we'll have to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can finish this now. I think it's probably a good idea if we just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd be happy to continue, but could I indicate that I have one or two questions arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might have one or two questions as well. So therefore, how much time would that approximately take?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would have thought between five and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then perhaps it's better to have a break now. Mr. Fazliu, we are almost finished but not completely. Therefore, we have a break and we'll finish after the break. We resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises to the parties and to you, Mr. Fazliu, but we had urgent matters to discuss which took us ten minutes more than we expected. We are in private session, Mr. Emmerson, do we have to remain in private session for your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have just got one. I just wanted to get an answer to the second to last question. It won't take a moment if, Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I just wanted to ask you this question or rather get an answer to it, because I don't think you actually addressed your mind to the question I was asking, it was a very simple one. All I was asking you is this: As you and your travelling companion were passing through Jablanica, did the question arise as between you of possibly staying, taking refuge, in Jablanica? That's all. Did it come up as a topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't discuss this because he had already made up his mind as to where he wanted to go. So I didn't intervene to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I just want to clarify one or two matters you've been asked about both by Judge Orie and by Mr. Di Fazio. First of all, first topic I want to return to, is Judge Orie asked you about an answer that you had given where you said that, in essence, you had offered to do some work around the house of Tal Zeka, but Tal Zeka insisted that you remain in the oda. Now, you told us, in answer to Judge Orie's question that it wasn't that he was insisting that you remain in the oda but that he was telling you, in effect, as a guest, it was not necessary for you to work. You remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, first of all, Tal Zeka's house was chosen as your destination not by you but by your travelling companion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tal Zeka was your travelling companion's relative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's a friend of the cousin of my travelling companion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you told us that Tal Zeka had said to you that as your -- as his guests, it wasn't necessary for you to work. Is it customary in Kosovar Albanian society for guests to remain in the oda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again just so it's absolutely clear, were you being detained in the oda? Or were you free to leave, if you wished to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was free, if I wanted to go somewhere, nobody prevented me. The owner just put up that reception for us as a sign of generosity. You know, he didn't -- he regretted it [as interpreted] to make me go out and work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly, Mr. Di Fazio asked you about a passage in the witness statement that you gave to the ICTY investigators in October 2005 referring to concerns that if people knew you'd made a statement, you would fall from grace, and he took you to a passage in the statement that you made to the Defence investigators in which you indicated that that was not a concern and had not been said by you. I just want to be clear about one matter, because just over six months before the Prosecution investigators spoke to you, you had given this interview or series of interviews you tell us to the media on about the 15th of March; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave one interview only, but it was relayed by three different dailies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So one interview published in three different places. And if you look in the file again, at tab 1, that interview is recorded as having been given on the 14th of March and published on the 15th of March of 2005. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I take it if that's the case, the translation tells us that it's, what's the date of publication? Unfortunately, the original either it's hidden behind the numbering or but there is no date on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think there is the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not the year. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I think you can confirm, can you, Mr. Fazliu, that this interview was given just after the indictment was made public, the same year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that. I wouldn't have had to make such an explanation had I not been obliged to shut the mouth of those gossip mongers who spread these rumours, that's why I had to make this explanation to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What's important for us to be clear about is to make sure that we have the right date for it. It's recorded in the original as an interview that took place during March, but in the original publication, it doesn't-- we can't see from our copy of it which year it was. Now, we know the indictment in this case was made public in March 2005 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I just mentioned it because there is no problem with it, I would say, because he couldn't comment on an indictment which doesn't exist, and then of course, in October he was interviewed and it was only later that he gave the interview to the Defence. So as far as the year is concerned, I just put it in for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What I'm concerned about is that this statement had been made six months before the OTP investigator spoke to him. As long as that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in the last sentence of the article which we didn't deal with before, you are recorded as having said this: It says, "According to Mr. Fazliu, he has given these clarifications not because he was scared or under pressure but in order for the truth to come out in this case." Did you say that when you were interviewed and is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the office in Kline at the office for information, 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when we come to the witness statement that you made in October 2005, when you were interviewed by the Prosecution investigators, I'm not going to ask for it to be brought up unless it becomes necessary, but in that witness statement, you give the names of certain people who you saw at Jabllanice. For example, you name Lahi and Nazmi Brahimaj as people who were at Jabllanice, but there is no suggestion in your witness statement to the Prosecution that you saw Ramush Haradinaj at Jabllanice. Now, obviously we know that in March of 2005, you had told the press that Ramush Haradinaj was not at Jabllanice. The question I want to ask you is can you remember now whether the investigators from the Prosecution asked you one way or the other if Ramush Haradinaj was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me, and I always gave the same answer, namely that he was not there and I'm certain of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that is something which they then must have failed to record in your witness statement; is that correct? Because there is nothing in your witness statement on the subject one way or the other, the Prosecution statement, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not my fault if they didn't write down what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, it wasn't your fault. Next, did they tell you that your travelling companion had made an allegation that whilst you were there, a 15 year old boy had had his ear cut off? Did they tell you that, the Prosecution investigators, because there is no mention of that in your Prosecution witness statement either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This question too was asked of me, but my answer is not there, and it is the same answer that I gave through the statement I gave to the Defence and which I confirmed here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally this: When you were then later interviewed by investigators for the Defence in June 2006 I just wanted to clarify one matter. You mentioned my name in connection with that statement. You were in fact I think interviewed, were you not, by a British female police officer together with a Kosovar Albanian called Isak Faro [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I thought that before the talk, they mentioned your name. I thought that they had come on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well they may well have said that to you. But just to be absolutely clear, Mr. Fazliu, before you came to court yesterday, you and I had never met, had we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Those are my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, just one matter for clarification. In your question at least you made an observation about interview by a police officer. I take it not a British police officer functioning as such, or a former police officer working as an investigator for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I understood it well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No additional questions arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No additional questions for you, Mr. Guy-Smith? Yes, Judge Hoepfel has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let me go back to that walk from Zhabel to Jablanica. What is the distance about between the two places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it takes you one hour, if you walk on foot. I never measured the time or the distance, but you have to walk rather fast. If you walk slowly, it may take you longer than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly, you walked slower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We walked very slow, as if we have -- we have a saying which says as if you count your own steps. And all along the way we talked. We talked as if we were going on a picnic. It was a rather very slow walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You said something like that yesterday also, and I didn't really understand because of these motivations you mentioned yesterday to get to Jablanica. You said two things which were urgent reasons for you to get to Jablanica. One was your brother in the hospital and the other one was the mobilisation issue. Do I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Today you said you learned only later that your brother was in the hospital. When did you learn that actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were talking about the date, the 20th, which was not clear to me before I arrived to Zhabel late in the evening. During the day of the 20th, I had no information on my brother's being wounded, but in the evening of the day, of the same day, when I arrived there at 11.00 at night, I heard from people who came there that he was wounded and was being treated in Jabllanice at the headquarters. And this is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Who told you that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people from the village who came there after us and during the day, they moved about, and that was -- there was also Sadri Berisha, and the leader of the village, who lived in another house in Zhabel, and it was through him that I got this information. If I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So forgive me for asking, but I don't really understand why you then took such a slow pace on your walk from one place to the other, from Zhabel to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why should we hurry up? Didn't have any motive to do that. Nobody forced us to move faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you mean with saying you walked arms in arms? With whom did you walk arms in arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With commander of Zhabel village, Tahir, that's his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whereas my companion, we talked all along the way. I stated this earlier. He asked me what my profession was, what I was doing, and then I asked him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The question was why you walked hand in hand or arm in arm, as you said. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see any reason why not. We got to know each other there. We were introduced there. And it was quite natural to us to learn something more about the private life of each other. Whereas my companion walked ahead of us with Ali and Fadil. They too were talking as they walked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Were they also arms in arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were side by side, like in a line, and this is how they walked, besides each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So your companion was not arms in arms with anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Fadil, Selmani and Ali Berisha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What, pardon? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My companion walked alongside Fadil Berisha and -- Selmani and Ali Berisha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was not my question. Pardon, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness might remove his headphones for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should take off your headphones for a second, Mr. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it may be that the words "arm in arm" are a colloquial Kosovo Albanian expression. I don't know if you would wish to explore whether he means literally "arm in arm" or whether that is an expression intended to mean walking side by side. I'm not certain what the answer is, but I understand that it is a colloquial expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fazliu -- thank you. Please maybe for clarification once more, what do you mean by you having walked arm in arm with Mr. Tahir, and the other group was walking side by side? Is that a difference or what do you want to express by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The expression "arm by arm", the way I understand it is if you are in good company and you feel comfortable, you can walk freely and hold all sorts of conversations. This is how I understand this expression, in good company, without any kind of hesitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I would have a few questions for you. First of all you said that you learned from the press about the name of Ujku perhaps being Pjeter. What did they write about him in the press? What was the reason that his name appeared in the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it appeared that he raised an accusation against Mr. Haradinaj, the former Prime Minister of Kosovo. It was something along those lines. I cannot be more accurate, but I think that was the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is, from what I understand you stayed for a couple of weeks, four weeks, in Maznik, after you had returned from Jablanica. Now, what did you do after those four weeks? Did you return to your village or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every third -- second or third day, I went back to the village, and I stayed there for the whole day sometimes, and then went back to Maznik in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did I understand you well that you stayed for four weeks in Maznik? Do you mean that you returned to Grabanica during those four weeks or that you extended your presence in Maznik even after that, although, going to Grabanica for perhaps two days a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that we stayed and slept in Maznik, and we helped out in that family where we stayed, but during the day, on certain days, we went with the son of Avdiv [phoen] even to Maliseva [phoen], and we also went to Grabanice because some families of Grabanice stayed there all the time. And after spending a few hours there, we went back to Maznik. And after four weeks in Maznik, then we moved to Kosuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you ever participate after those four weeks or even within those four weeks, did you ever participate in any military-like or operation? I mean did you ever carry an arm during that period? Were you ever involved in operations for whatever organisation, KLA, any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During our stay in Kosuric, we had guard duties with the KLA soldiers in the village, not only me but my other three, four brothers, and that was whenever we were given a timetable for doing this guard duties, and I was doing the guard duties in the area round Kosuric and that happened up until the moment when Kosuric was attacked, when we then withdrew from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fazliu, you answered my question. Then once you had left Jabllanice when, for the first time after you had come to Maznik did you meet Mr. Brahimaj, Mr. Lahi Brahimaj again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I went to Maznik, I met him because I went on several occasions to Jabllanice, and I met him two, three times, but it was after several -- several weeks, then I asked him to give me back my weapon and that's how I got it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say after several weeks. Is that the weapon you used when you were performing your guard duties, later, as you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Hungarian automatic rifle, Kalashnikov. It was that one. It was my weapon and it was returned to me as we had agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, yes. You said that was after a couple of weeks. My question was whether that was the weapon you used when standing guard, not what the weapon was, because that was an AK-47, as far as I understand, but did you use that weapon when standing guard after leaving Maznik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have used the same weapon to perform my guard duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the statement which was read to you, the statement given to the ICTY investigator, you said that the weapon was returned five or six months later. Have you corrected that when you spoke to the Defence where -- I'm just.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour it's -- again, it might be wiser if the witness removed his ear phones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there is anything of the kind, then please, if you give me a number, then I can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honour would just give me a moment. He corrected it both in his Defence statement and in his interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I overlooked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in his interview with Mr. Di Fazio where he said the six months should have read six weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I overlooked that and we can proceed. Then I do understand that you corrected that although I -- now, I do understand that you corrected that in your statement. I have one final question for you. You told in the statement you gave to the Defence that you learned that -- and let me take it literally. You said about your travel companion, "I heard he had gone to the USA." Could you tell us when did you hear that? Apparently prior to giving this statement in June 2006. Do you remember when you heard that and how you heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The son of one of his brothers in the village, that's how we heard about it, before he left for America he had said that he wanted to go there. But later on, when the son of his brother, Jefer [phoen], he told us he was somewhere in America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that before or after you gave the interview to the press, you remember that we -- that was March 2005. Was it prior to that that you heard that he had gone to the United States or was it after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that I heard about it after that date. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not sure about it. Thank you very much for that answer. Did the questions trigger any further need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Nothing arising, save to indicate to Your Honours' the answer to Your Honour's question. A correction will be found in the penultimate line of the second full paragraph on page 4 of the statement, and during the proofing session with Mr. Di Fazio, on page 22, when that paragraph was put to him, the witness is recorded as saying, "You are mistaken that I said months. It was weeks because five or six months would have been a very long time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have checked that Mr. Emmerson. First of all if you say that as a solid response then I. [Speakers overlapping].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I start from the points of view that you've checked that carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly, I wonder whether tabs 1 and 2 could please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, tab 1 would be the newspaper article dated the 15th of March with on top of it Kline 14th of March 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm being reminded that we should perhaps for this purpose go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could go to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the newspaper article under tab 1, is it uploaded already? It's uploaded already in e-court. Would have what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be Exhibit number D154 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then under tab 2, the statement of the witness dated the 15th of June 2006 would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be Exhibit number D155 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't ask for tab 3 to be marked for identification because I don't seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, as far as the status of tab 2 is concerned, we earlier discussed it to be perhaps an answer to your statement. Of course, 92 ter, there is one respect it starts from the assumption that the witness is called by the party who presents the statement as a 92 ter statement and that the witness is available for cross-examination. Here, however, the situation is slightly different, but I think on the basis of the ratio of Article 92 ter, that the Article would not oppose against admitting a statement under 92 ter where the witness is available for examination-in-chief. If that would be -- if the parties take any different view, then the Chamber would like to hear that later. Mr. Fazliu, first of all perhaps we directly deal with the exhibits. Mr. Di Fazio, I think we have dealt with all the P exhibits, that was only the marked map from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have two Defence exhibits any objections either the newspaper article --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, there is none. And I have no objection to them going into evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then exhibits D154 and D155 are admitted into evidence. The P exhibit was already admitted at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour addresses the witness, I wonder if we might go very briefly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fazliu, this concludes your evidence in this Court. You've been here for two days, many questions were put to you, they have been long sessions. I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and to answer questions of both parties and the Bench and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to see how far we come with shortening our list of exhibits on which no decisions have yet been taken. First of all, is there any new information the Chamber should hear about the five exhibits that were -- remained undetermined as far as Professor Dunjic is concerned, that's 746, 763, 774, 779 and 815.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre and I are still in the process of dealing with that issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will hear about that at a later stage. The parties have received this rather long list. As far as Witness 6 is concerned, I do understand that D114 was not dealt with out of oversight. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, no objection but, no, but D114 is a Defence Exhibit. Of course, you could -- we do not make any distinction between which Defence counsel, although I would invite Defence counsel, if one Defence counsel tenders any documents where other Defence counsel would object, I'd like to know that immediately and not wait until a couple of weeks after that. Then P335 was a matter of translation. Is the translation meanwhile completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They were redone by the official translation body, and I believe they are uploaded into e-court and are they now ready to be fully admitted as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true for the other counsel as well? Then P335 is admitted into evidence. We now come to a couple of exhibits tendered through witness Bajcetic, that is D130 through D -- at this moment, D136. I know that there are three more on the list, but I would first limit it to these Defence exhibits. That's D130 through D136. Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not to D130, 131, 132, 133 and 134 and 136. However, there is an objection to D135, which purports to be or is an extract from the Milutinovic pre-trial brief and the Prosecution is at a loss to see how it is relevant to these proceedings and awaits to hear the Defence's submissions on relevance so we can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's relevant because it deals with the Prosecution's position that General Colonel Vlastimir Djurdjevic was an architect of a plan to conceal evidence by moving bodies to frustrate the investigations of the Tribunal which in itself is relevant given the upcoming testimony of a witness whose protected status is yet to be determined, that General Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic was involved in the canal investigation and was one of the first at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether he was or not, of course, we do not know yet, but we'll consider this -- you would like to hear the relevance and then take a position, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure we have heard the relevance. The Prosecution in my general response at the moment is that it's -- for a start Mr. Emmerson hasn't pointed to the relevant passage, even a relevant footnote. It's a pre-trial brief, a position in relation to another case at a different time period involving different parties in a different area. It appears on its face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It certainly isn't evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It raised an interesting question, whether any perception expressed by any member of the Office of the Prosecution in another case emphasising a perception of what might be the truth, or to what extent that -- because that's just presenting on what they think they could prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in that context being relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It raises an interesting question. The short response is that the Office of the Prosecutor being indivisible, the Prosecution's position is not one of perception but one in which it makes allegations and accusations. And it's not in our submission open to the Prosecution to take a different position in two different cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that and see whether we ask further submissions on whether consistency in all cases under all circumstances is required from the Prosecution. But let's leave it at this moment. We are trying at this moment to cut short our list. Then D130 through D134 are admitted into evidence. D135 is pending. D136 is -- Mr. Re I think you said something about D135. I asked comments until D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: D135 was the one was the one I was objecting to which was the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm now talking about D136. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D136 is admitted into evidence. As far as D137 through D139 is concerned, these are statements on which the Chamber would like to -- the Defence to reconsider whether it wants to tender it in light of the recent decisions on admission into evidence of statements which were obtained specifically for the purpose of information, witness information, for these proceedings. So the Chamber would very much like the Defence to see whether it still tenders it and is not satisfied with just the quotes used in court. Then we move to the next witness, a similar reconsideration will be required from the Defence as far as D91 is concerned. The Chamber would like to hear from that from the Defence. Then the next one is P376, Pekka Haverinen being the witness. Redactions had to be made, redactions have been made meanwhile, I think that apart from these redactions to be made there were no objections. Then P376 is admitted into evidence. We move on to the next one, that's P367. Yes, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is a pending issue in respect of that statement. I raised at the conclusion of the witness's testimony. Your Honour will recall that that witness gave evidence at a time prior to the current procedure having been established in respect of 92 ter witness statements that objections be exchanged and then rulings sought. And I had indicated that there was a passage in the witness's consolidated witness statement to which I took objection but which was not elicited from the witness in evidence-in-chief. And now is not the time to deal with the matter. It will take a little while. But it relates to the extent of the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the redaction required? Because I remember that the redaction required had something to do with that as well. I mean the redaction was not protection but was a portion inappropriate to be introduced through 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it was not but may we check the position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It relates essentially to the witness's ability to describe the age of a tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll then perhaps -- let's not at this moment lose time on this in court. The Chamber would like to be informed about the redacted 92 ter statement of Pekka Haverinen and to see whether the objection you just raised still stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's my fault. If I've misled Your Honour, I was referring to 367 which I thought Your Honour had moved on to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I thought you had. Number 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's almost the same number. That's 3 -- perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour may have misspoken. That's why I was on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you went too fast. I was starting P367 not saying anything about it yet, and then you started already because for 367, I would have referred to some confusion as far as the admission of this statement is concerned. I think it is page -- I think it's page 5992 in which, by the way also there is a mistake, because it says something about 73 ter rather than 93 ter. Where Mr. Dutertre -- but even there I could not exclude for the possibility of a translation error. I'm always surprised that there is so little, as a matter of fact, where he said there he said, "because we have admitted this statement under Article 73 ter," might have been that it is submitted. There seems to be some unclarity as to whether the 92 ter statement was admitted because there is no formal admission there and since I do understand that there still is an objection in relation to that, the Chamber would like to hear, as soon as possible, about 367 and just to put things right on the record, where we admitted P376, that's the Pekka Haverinen statement, that admission is final. So then we move on to D41, in relation to Rrustem Tetaj, where the OTP reserved its right to object but we have heard of no objection since. It's the videoclip.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I have a question before giving a decision on that. It's described as a videoclip showing the swearing-in ceremony in Beranj dated the 20th of July, and then who they swore in, a large number of volunteers. That's a nice description of part of the video. The video as it was delivered and as it was uploaded as far as I understand contains far more. It contains meetings, training sessions, all kind of other things apart from the swearing in ceremony with a large number of people present, a lot of signing, et cetera. But there is certainly on that video, as we have it, there is far more on it. So therefore I'd like to, before we admit it into evidence, we'd like the Defence to check whether this exhibit is really limited to this and then provide a new copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or to explain why all the other parts are in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The short answer is that that was the form in which the videotape was disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution. But the only passage that was played and relied upon in evidence and upon which the witness was questioned is the passage that was described in the descriptive paragraph and therefore, we will ask the audiovisual unit to cut the video to that passage and have that substituted for the video that's on the exhibit at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the page in e-court describes it in this way, and we have to be sure that the video which finally is handed over to the registrar is the video containing only that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We will make arrangements for it to be edited in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I see that as far as Bogdan, Tomas is concerned, we still have an objection by the OTP of which I don't have the details at this moment, so I'd rather leave that for a moment. Otherwise there would be no list left at all. Next one Radovan Zlatkovic, I do understand that there is an issue raised in respect not of the 92 statement itself but only in relation to annex 10 to that. That would be P864. Is that correctly understood? There is an issue taken on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that there have been appropriate redactions made to the 92 ter statement, so with that in mind there is no objection with regard to the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to, I believe that there were objections both to annex 10 and with regard to annex 11, it was agreed that annex 11 would not be part of this particular 92 ter statement and was taken out in toto is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is here that the annexes received separate numbers. And so therefore, 865, Mr. Re, if it's not clear to you that's no problem, then we have identified where the problems are, they remain on the list, all the others are removed from the list. May I then take it that P864, being annex 10 to the 92 ter statement, and P865, which is annex 11 to the 92 ter statements, that we'll further hear from whether they are withdrawn, whether they are still objections pending?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Dutertre and Mr. Guy-Smith can maybe work something out on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So P864 and P865 are still on the list. There are, from what I understand, there are no objections raised against P854 which is the 92 ter statement through P863 which is the annexes up to and including annex 9 to the 92 ter statement. No objections, admitted into evidence. Then we have P866 through P883, all annexes to the -- all annexes to the 92 ter statement of Radovan Zlatkovic. Any objections? Then P866 through P883 are admitted into evidence. Finally in relation to Witness Zlatkovic, on the list D153 which is an RDB official note, perhaps should have been on the list, admission not being determined yet. If the Prosecution would like to take its time to see what it is, fine. Otherwise, we'll decide on the admission. I think we look at the clock. D153 still is on the list. All the other items on the list are not to be discussed at this very moment. We will -- I think the interpreters and technicians and transcribers, but also security for these additional minutes not requested but implicitly granted. I feel a bit guilty. We will adjourn. We are not sitting on Monday.
